meta.session_title: Day 1 - Introduction to Java & Language Fundamentals
meta.pedagogy: Hands-on learning with step-by-step guidance. Each exercise builds on the previous. All concepts from the session are coded. Banking/finance examples used for context.

objectives: Use all 8 Java primitive types in a meaningful context and understand their sizes, ranges, and appropriate use cases.
prerequisites: IntelliJ IDEA (Community Edition) or VS Code with Java Extension
Git installed and GitHub account created

exercises.title: Primitive Data Types — Bank Account Record
exercises.objective: Use all 8 Java primitive types in a meaningful context and understand their sizes, ranges, and appropriate use cases.
exercises.scenario: Model a bank account record using the most appropriate Java primitive type for each field. This is the foundation of data modeling in any banking system.
instructions: Step 1: Create a new Java class called 'BankAccountRecord' in the same project
Step 2: Declare one variable for each of the 8 primitive types (see starter code)
Step 3: Print each variable using System.out.printf for formatted output
Step 4: Add a TASK comment where indicated and complete each task
Step 5: Run and verify your output matches the expected output
Step 6: EXPERIMENT — what happens when you assign 200 to a byte? What error do you get?
Step 7: EXPERIMENT — what does Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 print? Can you explain why?
exercises.expected_output:
========== Bank Account Details ==========
Account Number  : 9876543210
Branch Code     : 1042
Transaction Count: 1500
KYC Status      : 2 (0=Pending, 1=Submitted, 2=Verified)
Balance         : 150000.75
Interest Rate   : 8.5%
Account Type    : S
Is Active       : true

========== Primitive Ranges ==========
Byte max     : 127
Short max    : 32767
Int max      : 2147483647
Long max     : 9223372036854775807

========== Overflow Experiment ==========
Integer.MAX_VALUE     : 2147483647
Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 : -2147483648

========== Floating-Point Precision ==========
0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004
== 0.3 ? false
BigDecimal 0.1+0.2 = 0.3
== 0.3 ? true
hints: The 'L' suffix in 9876543210L tells Java this is a long literal (without 'L', Java reads integer literals as int, causing compile error for numbers > 2.1 billion)
Underscores in numbers (1_500, 1_50_000.75) are allowed from Java 7+ — they only affect readability, not the value
BigDecimal constructor takes a String argument, NOT a double. new BigDecimal(0.1) still has precision issues!
reflection_questions: Why is int insufficient for storing phone numbers? Which type would you use?
A bank transaction might store an amount like ₹99,99,999.99 — which type(s) would you consider and why?
What would happen if a banking system used int (not long) for account balances and a customer had ₹22 crore in their account?
exercises.debugging_task: Deliberately introduce this bug and observe the error: byte buggy = 200; What does the compiler say? Change it to short — does it work?
